What the original study did not say

Vaccines and autism: the story of a fraud

A 1998 article about twelve children sparked a fear that still persists. It was retracted and its author lost his medical licence.

In 1998, the British doctor Andrew Wakefield published a study in The Lancet on twelve children with bowel and developmental problems, and suggested at a press conference that the MMR vaccine might be linked to autism.

The fraud

The journalist Brian Deer found that Wakefield had manipulated the children's data and had conflicts of interest: he was being paid by lawyers preparing lawsuits against vaccine makers. In 2010, The Lancet retracted the article and Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register.

Since then, studies of millions of children, such as a 2019 Danish study of more than 650,000, have found no link between the vaccine and autism. But the fear lowered vaccination rates in several countries and measles outbreaks returned. It shows how a false idea, told convincingly, can be very hard to correct.

References

  1. Godlee, F., Smith, J. y Marcovitch, H. (2011). Wakefield's article linking MMR vaccine and autism was fraudulent. BMJ, 342, c7452.
  2. Hviid, A. et al. (2019). Measles, mumps, rubella vaccination and autism: a nationwide cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine, 170(8), 513–520.
